summary.text: Take the counterexample \(n=8\): Möbius inversion gives \(a(8)=8!(H_8-H_4)=25584>0\), since the terms involving \(\mu(8)\) and \(\mu(4)\) vanish. But \(8=2^3\), so \(\Omega(8)=3\) is odd and at least \(3\), contradicting the asserted equivalence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m \frac1j
\]
denote the \(m\)-th harmonic number. The sequence is defined by
\[
\sum_{k\mid n}\frac{a(k)}{k!}=H_n
\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
Put \(b(k)=a(k)/k!\). Then the defining relation says
\[
\sum_{k\mid n}b(k)=H_n.
\]
By Möbius inversion,
\[
b(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)H_d,
\]
and hence
\[
a(n)=n!\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)H_d,
\]
where \(\mu\) is the Möbius function.

We disprove the conjecture with the positive integer
\[
n=8.
\]
First consider the conjecture's condition involving the number of prime factors. Since
\[
8=2^3,
\]
the total number of prime factors counted with multiplicity is
\[
\Omega(8)=3.
\]
Thus \(\Omega(8)\) is odd and is at least \(3\). Consequently, the right-hand side of the proposed equivalence
\[
a(8)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(\Omega(8)\text{ is odd and }\Omega(8)\ge 3\bigr)
\]
is true.

It remains to compute the sign of \(a(8)\). The positive divisors of \(8\) are
\[
1,2,4,8.
\]
Therefore the Möbius-inversion formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(8)
 &=8!\left(\mu(8)H_1+\mu(4)H_2+\mu(2)H_4+\mu(1)H_8\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The needed Möbius values are
\[
\mu(8)=0,\qquad \mu(4)=0,\qquad \mu(2)=-1,\qquad \mu(1)=1.
\]
Indeed, \(4\) and \(8\) are divisible by the square \(2^2\), so their Möbius values are zero; \(2\) is a product of one distinct prime, so its Möbius value is \(-1\); and by definition \(\mu(1)=1\). It follows that
\[
a(8)=8!\,(H_8-H_4).
\]
The difference of the harmonic numbers consists exactly of the terms from \(1/5\) through \(1/8\):
\[
H_8-H_4=\frac15+\frac16+\frac17+\frac18.
\]
Using the common denominator \(840\),
\[
\frac15+\frac16+\frac17+\frac18
 =\frac{168+140+120+105}{840}
 =\frac{533}{840}.
\]
Since \(8!=40320\) and \(40320/840=48\), we obtain
\[
a(8)=40320\cdot\frac{533}{840}=48\cdot533=25584.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(8)=25584>0,
\]
so the assertion \(a(8)<0\) is false.

Thus, at \(n=8\), the condition “\(\Omega(n)\) is odd and at least \(3\)” is true, whereas \(a(n)<0\) is false. The claimed equivalence therefore fails at the positive integer \(8\), disproving the universal conjecture.
